title: The Platform Engineering Playbook for Production LLMs
gist: A Walmart Global Tech engineer argues that LLM reliability is a platform problem: centralizing retries, schema enforcement, prompt versioning, intent gating, MCP-level authorization and per-team observability cut hallucinations in a production inventory agent from ~15% to 1.5% without changing the foundation model. The piece is a build-order playbook for enterprises scaling multi-team agent deployments.

themes.theme: Hallucination rate is a platform lever, not a model lever

insights.claim: In an enterprise inventory-recommendation multi-agent system, production hallucination rate fell from roughly 15% to 1.5% over six months through platform-level controls rather than a better foundation model.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Reliability gains in enterprise AI are accruing to the orchestration/platform layer, shifting value away from pure model upgrades.
insights.quote: the lever that moved the number wasn't a better foundation model
insights.locator: Six months later the rate was 1.5 percent

insights.claim: Most of the 15% to 1.5% reduction came from retry orchestration with validation that classifies failures into schema violations, hallucination signals and infrastructure errors, each handled differently.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Differentiated failure handling is the cheap, replicable mechanism; vendors selling guardrails or reliability tooling address a real, measurable gap.
insights.locator: Retry Orchestration with Validation

insights.claim: Blind retries are harmful: repeating a prompt that hallucinated yields a different hallucination, and naive retries during an outage create traffic storms that overload infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Naive retry defaults in agent frameworks can amplify provider outages and cost, which matters for rate-limited API consumers.
insights.quote: Blindly rerunning failed LLM calls is actively harmful.
insights.locator: Retry Orchestration with Validation

insights.claim: Schema violations are re-prompted with the validation error appended, hallucination signals with stronger grounding context, and infrastructure errors (429, 503) with exponential backoff, capped at three tries because a structured-output failure unfixed by the third try almost never fixes on the fourth.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete retry-budget heuristic (count, token or time cap) that bounds runaway inference spend.
insights.locator: Route by Class

insights.claim: Forcing the model to emit machine-readable grounded and out_of_scope flags costs nothing to generate yet turns vague hallucinations into typed, countable events; a response failing validation is described as the highest-precision hallucination signal a platform has.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Structured output with self-declared grounding is a low-cost evals primitive that enterprises can adopt immediately.
insights.locator: The grounded and out_of_scope flags

insights.claim: Grounding is framed as a pipeline, not a prompt trick: tools fetch the evidence, the prompt restricts the model to it, the schema forces a declaration, and validation converts a broken declaration into a counted, retryable failure.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Tool/retrieval access (MCP servers, docs lookup) becomes a reliability moat, favoring vendors that supply authoritative context.
insights.quote: Grounding here is not a prompt trick, it is a pipeline.
insights.locator: Grounding here is not a prompt trick

insights.claim: An intent-validation gate that returns 'unclassified' instead of defaulting to the highest-scoring agent prevents agents from handling questions they were not built for, and also shrinks the space the model must search, lowering hallucination and context size.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: A small, cheap classifier ahead of an expensive frontier-model call reduces both error rates and inference cost, favoring tiered model architectures.
insights.locator: Intent Validation as a Routing Gate

themes.theme: Case for a shared LLM platform layer

insights.claim: The decision point for building a shared LLM platform is the second application, not the first; by the time ten teams ship LLM features, retrofitting is a long and difficult migration.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Enterprise demand for LLM gateways/platform tooling arises early in adoption, supporting a buying window for infrastructure vendors.
insights.quote: The decision point for building this platform isn't the first LLM application. It's the second.
insights.locator: The decision point for building this platform

insights.claim: The shared concerns that justify centralization are retry/failure classification, prompt registry, schema enforcement, token cost attribution, behavioral observability, tool/context routing and authN/authZ across tool servers; each team otherwise rebuilds the same scaffolding.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Defines the product surface for an enterprise LLM platform and the categories where startups and hyperscalers compete.
insights.locator: For LLMs the shared concerns are

insights.claim: A shared platform forces a contract (applications declare model, prompt version, schema, tool set and eval engine; platform delivers it), which is what lets a new application reach production in days instead of months.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Platform contracts compress time-to-production, so productivity gains from AI show up first in organizations with strong platform teams.
insights.locator: There is a second-order effect

insights.claim: LLM failures at scale were rate-limiting by the model provider, bad context data rather than the model itself, and steady-rate hallucinations; the context failure made data-engineering pipelines central to the fix.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Provider throttling and data quality, not model capability, were the first production bottlenecks, favoring data-infrastructure spend.
insights.locator: In our case, three failures surfaced

insights.claim: The author predicts the shift from building an LLM application to building on an LLM platform is the one the rest of the field will make over the next two years, on its own timeline or under pressure from an incident.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Implies a two-year wave of enterprise platform spending on LLM gateways, registries, eval and observability tooling.
insights.locator: The shift from "we built an LLM application"

insights.claim: LLM systems let teams defer infrastructure decisions because they do not crash or return 500 errors; they quietly produce slightly worse output, so the gap between a wrong decision and its visible consequence makes retrofitting costly.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Silent degradation means AI-feature quality risk is under-priced by teams relying on traditional uptime metrics.
insights.quote: They do not crash. They do not return 500 errors. They quietly produce slightly worse output.
insights.locator: The unifying thread among these decisions

insights.claim: The stack is layered so the model (LiteLLM), tool (Model Context Protocol, FastMCP) and orchestration (Google's ADK) layers each sit behind stable interfaces, letting any one be swapped for a stronger model, different tool server or orchestrator without rewriting platform primitives.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Model-provider swappability via a gateway like LiteLLM weakens lock-in to any single foundation-model vendor.
insights.locator: The value of this separation

themes.theme: Prompt versioning and evaluation as release engineering

insights.claim: Prompts should be treated like code: every prompt gets an ID and version, is deployable independently of application code, and rolls back by repointing the active version at runtime without redeploying, since two prompts differing by one sentence can have meaningfully different hallucination rates, latency and token costs.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Prompt registries and rollback are emerging as standard LLMOps products; unmanaged prompt edits are a hidden operational risk.
insights.quote: Tweaking prompts without a clear audit trail is the easiest way to silently break your AI's behavior.
insights.locator: Key Takeaways

insights.claim: The companion repo's prompt registry is in-memory, which the author concedes is unsuitable for production; the production step is a database behind the same interface with separate version bindings per environment (dev, staging, prod).
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Shows the reference implementation is a teaching artifact, so production adopters still need persistence and environment promotion.
insights.locator: One honest limitation

insights.claim: Evaluation is a four-part gate: a golden set stored as data, a runner that executes the real agent several times per case and averages (because the model is stochastic), scored metrics, and a threshold; the repo requires average tool-trajectory score of at least 0.8.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Quantified eval gates tied to prompt promotion are the mechanism by which enterprises will govern agent changes.
insights.locator: The threshold is what makes it a gate

insights.claim: Fast hermetic tests gate merges on every push while model-backed evals run as a separate triggered job that gates prompt promotions, and every user-facing incident becomes a new golden-set case so the same failure cannot ship twice.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Separating cheap tests from costly live-model evals controls CI inference spend while still gating releases.
insights.locator: Two design choices make this effort worthwhile

themes.theme: Security: authorization at the MCP resource server

insights.claim: Authorization should be enforced at each MCP resource server with a strict default-deny policy rather than only at the gateway, because relying solely on gateway checks means any single orchestrator bug can expose every connected tool.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Agent-tool security is shifting toward per-tool zero-trust RBAC, creating demand for identity and policy tooling around MCP.
insights.quote: The decision I would defend hardest is where this policy is enforced.
insights.locator: The decision I would defend hardest

insights.claim: In multi-team deployments the more important agent-security problem is not prompt injection but plain RBAC: which caller role may invoke which team's tool; the platform issues stateless role-carrying JWTs and policies live in a YAML config so permission changes need no deployment.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Reframes enterprise agent risk from exotic attacks to ordinary access control, a more tractable and budgetable problem.
insights.quote: Most write-ups treat agent security as a prompt-injection problem.
insights.locator: Authentication and Authorization

themes.theme: Observability and cost attribution for LLMs

insights.claim: Standard APM (latency, error rate, throughput) shows only whether the model is reachable, not whether it behaves correctly, so teams must instrument hallucination rate, prompt drift, tool invocation patterns and sampled behavioral correctness; the author calls standard APM the most expensive thing they got wrong.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Traditional observability vendors must add semantic-quality metrics or cede an LLM-observability category to specialists.
insights.quote: Standard APM was the most expensive thing we got wrong.
insights.locator: Observability for LLMs

insights.claim: Without per-request attribution, model spend arrives as a single vendor line item and optimization is guesswork; the team dimension must exist in the data from the first call because it cannot be rebuilt from logs, and retrofitting costs weeks of engineering time.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Token cost attribution (FinOps for AI) is a gating requirement for scaling LLM budgets and a growing tooling niche.
insights.locator: The detail that makes "per team" work

insights.claim: Cost is recorded at every model call site via an after-model callback, so a request fanning out to four specialists attributes all four calls to the same user and team; metrics export through OpenTelemetry wrapped in custom methods so backends like Prometheus can be swapped.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Multi-agent fan-out multiplies per-request model calls, so cost accounting must be per call rather than per response.
insights.locator: Token cost is recorded at every model call site

insights.claim: A multi-agent pipeline needs a single coordinator owning the topology with circuit breakers and timeout budgets; otherwise agents independently retry the components above them and turn one isolated failure into a system-wide crash.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Retry storms between cooperating agents are a systemic reliability risk, and a driver of centralized orchestration products.
insights.locator: The agent coordinator pattern

insights.claim: The recommended build order is observability before the first production deployment, platform thinking before the second application, prompt versioning from day one, schema enforcement on the first call, cost tags on every request, and a golden-set eval per specialist before the first prompt change.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Gives a checklist for judging enterprise AI maturity and for diligencing teams that claim production-grade agent deployments.
insights.locator: the six concrete decisions, in priority order
